teaching.causalExplanation: The syllabus asks first what contemporary forms of exercise are: the newer ways people exercise, often outside traditional club sport. Group fitness classes remove the need for skill, because someone tells you what to do. Community runs and walks are free, weekly and open to anyone. There are bootcamps in parks, social and modified sport, and app-based challenges and online classes. And there's exercising alone, with a gym card or home gear, the most convenient form, and the one many people drop. The reason is in the design. Convenience removes other people. What the successful forms share isn't the exercise. It's the structure: a fixed time someone else set, a group that meets whether you feel like it or not, no skill needed to start, and people who'd notice if you weren't there. Inside a group, members shape each other. That's group dynamics, and its strongest tool is the norm, an unwritten rule about what people here do. If everyone finishes the session, finishing takes no decision, and stopping early does. Groups also hold together in two ways. Task cohesion is unity around a shared goal. Social cohesion is liking each other and valuing the time together, and it's strongly linked to turning up. Both are linked to performance. A group needs both. A team with a shared goal that dislikes each other performs while results hold, then fractures. A group that loves its coffee after training but shares no standard has fun, and doesn't improve. So a group that gets on well won't automatically perform. So why does B keep going? A group changes the decision itself. Skipping a solo session costs nothing, and nobody knows. Skipping when someone's waiting means letting a person down, and that cost arrives just when motivation is lowest. You don't have to enjoy a five-thirty alarm when someone's waiting for you. The group also keeps an if-then plan for you: Tuesday at six, in the park. It offers support: a lift, advice, company when it's hard. And it confirms the identity. Being named and expected by other runners makes I'm someone who runs feel true. That's belonging, being known, expected, and missed when you're not there. Now the hard answer. Welcome B for three weeks, then stop noticing, and she'll quietly drift away. A warm welcome brings people in. Being missed keeps them. One message to someone who didn't come is a real retention plan.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus asks first what contemporary forms of exercise are: the newer ways people exercise, often outside traditional club sport. Group fitness classes remove the need for skill, because someone tells you what to do. Community runs and walks are free, weekly and open to anyone. There are bootcamps in parks, social and modified sport, and app-based challenges and online classes. And there's exercising alone, with a gym card or home gear, the most convenient form, and the one many people drop. The reason is in the design. Convenience removes other people. What the successful forms share isn't the exercise. It's the structure: a fixed time someone else set, a group that meets whether you feel like it or not, no skill needed to start, and people who'd notice if you weren't there.

scenes.teachingReason: Inside a group, members shape each other. That's group dynamics, and its strongest tool is the norm, an unwritten rule about what people here do. If everyone finishes the session, finishing takes no decision, and stopping early does. Groups also hold together in two ways. Task cohesion is unity around a shared goal. Social cohesion is liking each other and valuing the time together, and it's strongly linked to turning up. Both are linked to performance. A group needs both. A team with a shared goal that dislikes each other performs while results hold, then fractures. A group that loves its coffee after training but shares no standard has fun, and doesn't improve. So a group that gets on well won't automatically perform.

scenes.teachingReason: So why does B keep going? A group changes the decision itself. Skipping a solo session costs nothing, and nobody knows. Skipping when someone's waiting means letting a person down, and that cost arrives just when motivation is lowest. You don't have to enjoy a five-thirty alarm when someone's waiting for you. The group also keeps an if-then plan for you: Tuesday at six, in the park. It offers support: a lift, advice, company when it's hard. And it confirms the identity. Being named and expected by other runners makes I'm someone who runs feel true. That's belonging, being known, expected, and missed when you're not there. Now the hard answer. Welcome B for three weeks, then stop noticing, and she'll quietly drift away. A warm welcome brings people in. Being missed keeps them. One message to someone who didn't come is a real retention plan.

scenes.teachingReason: Communities improve performance too, by four routes. The biggest is simply more practice: four years instead of four weeks. Second, norms set the standard. Train beside someone a bit better, and you work harder without being told. But it cuts both ways: if most people stop early, stopping early becomes normal. A group amplifies its norms. Third, tips and feedback get shared. Fourth, hard sessions are easier to finish with company. Two catches. Social facilitation: others watching helps a well-learned skill, but can hurt one you're still learning. And social loafing: people ease off when nobody can see their own effort, so make each person's contribution visible.

scenes.teachingReason: And an honest answer names the limits. A group that creates belonging also draws a boundary. If everyone looks alike in age, ability or background, others read it as not for them. Earlier, you saw access isn't only cost: a paid six am class with no early bus suits people with money, a car and a free morning. That's why free, local, volunteer-run events reach people commercial ones don't. Cohesion can also lock in harmful norms, like training through pain, because pushing back risks belonging. And if all your exercise lives in one group, it ends when the group does. So design communities deliberately.
